Игра "Battle Nations" - это захватывающая стратегическая игра, сочетающая в себе элементы градостроительства и пошаговых боев. Мне очень понравилось развивать свою базу, добывать ресурсы и тренировать разнообразных юнитов. Боевая система интуитивно понятна, но требует тактического мышления, особенно в PvP-сражениях. Разнообразие юнитов и возможность их прокачки придают игре глубину и позволяют экспериментировать с разными стратегиями.

Графика выполнена в приятном мультяшном стиле, неплохо смотрится на мобильных устройствах. Однако, стоит отметить, что игра довольно старая, и это заметно по некоторым аспектам UI и оптимизации. Но несмотря на это, игровой процесс остается увлекательным.
Главный минус, на мой взгляд, - довольно агрессивная монетизация. Прогресс без доната возможен, но потребует значительного времени и терпения. В целом, если вы любите стратегии и готовы к некоторой "гринд", "Battle Nations" может стать отличным способом скоротать время. Рекомендую, особенно если вас привлекает ретро-стиль.

This game is amazing. I have been playing it for nearly 2 years now and honestly have had an addiction to it, and still do! 
The bad reviews on this game are just premature. I completely agree the first 20 levels (which are very easy to surf through) are very boring and there isnt much to do. However, past these levels of introductions of characters, storylines and tutorials this game becomes a large, social haven. Of course after reaching level 65 (the current level cap) you would think there is nothing to do. This is not the case. There is even more to do. With the new Boss Strike events and invasions (frequently occuring) this game becomes part of its own league. You can play with your guild mates working together to achieve the common goals of special prizes and trophies in the guild system. Although there is room for improvement, this game has taken a lot of time up because of how diverse and global this game is. Granted, you would do better if you pay for the currency, but, this is not a Pay-2-win game. I have many friends who have never bought the currency and are still in high tier guilds enjoying the game to its fullest. Paying does make the game go quicker and makes it more enjoyable, however, but isnt this the same with all games? You pay you get a small advantage - an advantage that isnt needed to do the best. 
So, give this game a chance. Guranteed after level 35 you will be playing your socks off :)
Give it a shot, you won't be disappointed.

I have long waited for this game to come back since its departure in 2016. The story of how this game was acquired back from King (Developers of Candy Crush) and formerly owned by Z2 (before King bought them) is nothing short of incredible. 

The fans brought this game back and it took nearly a decade of hard work. This is just a beta with the intention to bring the game back to its original status before the shutdown and continue to create new content for it. The patreon really is a means to support this independent developer to make the game. They gambled on the risk to revive the IP and acquire it from an evil company (King) to own the rights to it. If you can't afford to jump on the beta then just wait for the full release. There is close to 4k supporters on the patreon right now. This game will move towards a full release where you can all play it then.  

Having spent 100's of hours on the original game I can confidently say this is something that will come to fruition. The community is there and has stayed intact all these years since the games first inception in 2012. 

Paying for the Patreon will give you early access to the game and get a head start when it fully releases to the public. 

If you have never played this game then its understandable to be hesitant to support it and I would encourage to look at the discord channel for the game to learn more about it to make that educated decision on your own. 

As of now most of the legacy story content is available in the beta and going forward they are working to bring back multiplayer and raids which was the thing that drove the community back in the day to be extremely addicted to this game.

As for gameplay its a turn-based strategy / City Development Sim. It is meant to be accessible as a mobile game and obviously on steam too. Building your Base and Army will take real world time to produce materials/troops/expansion etc. then you can battle other armies as you progress through the game to level up your army troops.

If you don't like the real world time aspect to build or heal units then it may be something to consider before buying the game. 

Personally the strategy that evolves from this game is so unique because you have a bunch of different classes and types of soldiers/vehicles/aircraft/boats that can be used in combination when battling. Its what keeps the addiction of playing this game going. 

Anyways play the game for yourself or look up videos but you can catch me building my base in this game until full release in anticipation of what will come.

THE GAME IS BACK! Here's my review from 2014:

I played this game for about 2 years on iOS.
Would people please stop giving off your misleading, useless spam reviews. First off; it isn't p2w. P2w means Pay-to-win. What does that mean? P2w is when a game offers game-breaking premium content that gives payers insane advantages and the game is near hopeless without it.

HAVING CONTENT THAT SIMPLY LOOKS NICER ISN'T "WINNING". I have put money in over the years; so lets' compare the content I have to free stuff; the distillery(free, game-resources) is critical to some missions and doesn't give out any extra money compared to the brewery(premium). The cobblestone roads look nicer, and give mildy bigger tax returns compared to the blacktop road(free). Even in decorations, premium only gives more variety. The artworks aren't even all that far apart in style. Premium units are inferior to special units you can get with a good guild and participation in boss battles, heck, you can even EARN premium credits from boss strikes with your guild.
Before you go on to complain about the defenses being superior, just actually build a garrison and a couple blockhouses, you'll find there isn't much of an issue with defense. AT ALL in fact. I just have the armored fortress(premium) again, because it looks imposing.

Another thing is when people accuse it of being a FB game or like one.

You DON'T spam your friends or post stupid things to your wall. Get a guild and add them; no adding to friends or spam invites necessary, and actually, kind of impossible.

There IS a player base. There are TONS of full guilds at level 50 with some 60-70 members, tons of them. Just look at the leaderboards. No one played PVP because there isn't a lobby system and the level (and would you believe LOCATION) threshhold is very tight. Finding someone your exact level and nearby within' 30 seconds isn't exactly the easiest thing to match up. Besides, PvP isn't that fun.


ON TO MY REVIEW INSTEAD OF COUNTERPOINTS:

The game itself is very well done with lots of good, story-driven missions. Destroying Gantas's fortress, battling the legendary Ridgy Didgy, to finding the ancient stucture, is all very well written. Although challenging at times, you can just leave the missions be for a while and move on with the game until you can compete against them.

If money is a problem, then you probably need to upgrade your structures and add decorations. Plus, having roads and a good layout gives you an advantage. I'm sick of 'similar'(if they can even be compared to) games encouraging the bunching together of structures with outlaying defenses. Having cluttered defenses does nothing as only so many can participate in battle. Garrisons and defenses have long ranges and you'll find that outposts that look liek military bases, cities, or settlements, are far superior in defense and profit when compared the the FaceBook jockeys who bunch together their buildings in a center surrounded by defenses and walls (Occupy these guys; easy money).

The combat system is a turn-based system. To master it, you need to have a variation in defense. Tanks are good fodder, but don't hit as hard as a lot of other units. You can earn Air Force units, which are hard to target in themselves, by joining an active guild and participating in boss strikes. The mercenary vault also gets some good units, which are great for occuption and raiding.

Building takes patience, and most of your tiem will be spent reorganizng your buildings to get the best look as possible. I for one have a city-style outpost. I have a sector for commercial-looking buildings, a residential area(middle class) an upper-class area, and a shanty town. The industreal sector doesn't have cobblestone roads, but I like blacktop roads better for my industry. I also have a park, a military base, an agriculture region with an orchard and field, as well as a tent city. The area (excluding the tents and agriculture) is surrounded by concrete walls with guard posts at the entry ways.

If you've heard people call Battle Nations essentially a FaceBook game... it is. Sort of. Worth more than those things, but that comparison is not at all far off.

I would say that its strengths come from its characterization of the atmosphere. The actual characters in particular are written in fairly interesting ways and have vast amounts of dialogue. Some of it is quite funny, most of it quite engaging. Items and actions often have amusing descriptions, and there are a number of things to do during a play session. If you're a fan of resource-collecting, I suppose there's something you'll find here. There's lotsa that. The combat system was something I found to be very fun. If you've ever played Final Fantasy: Tactics or other tile-combat-ish games, they hold many similarities. Plus, if you like Team Fortress 2, apparently some of the more notable characters, i.e. the Heavy and the Pyro, are in Battle Nations. I suppose that's not much of a selling point, but I thought I'd mention it 'cause that's pretty much the only reason I got Battle Nations in the first place.

But weaknesses? There are a lot to be sure. While there's no arbitrary energy system like in many city-building FaceBook games, there are many moments when you just have to either wait and do absolutely jack-diddly or do a few repetitive tasks, i.e. waiting five minutes for cabbages. Yeah, it's a real-time game. Set something up and wait actual minutes for it to finish. I personally like those because of how I play games, but I know a lot of people don't. Granted, there are a lot of timers that are fairly short, taking literally what barely makes several seconds (building some things only takes three seconds), but there are a number of things that also take a whole ruddy day to finish. The humor, if you play it very often, can get wearing after a time. The art, while I appreciate its uniqueness, is kind of bizarre and definitely is not gonna be everyone's cuppa. I rather like it, but even then, it's more of an "Oh, it's neat that it looks like that" than an "I really like the way that looks." I'm talking mostly about the talking heads, but the rest of the art falls into this category too at times.

In addition, I don't know if anyone else has this problem, but I can't complete of the missions in the game because the game decides to have a crash whenever I look at the forces' Unit screen. I rarely run into game-breaking bugs, and I don't know if this qualifies as such as I can still play the rest of the game pretty alright, but that's a whole mission I can't complete. And because it's a whole screen I can't access without the game crashing, that's a whole level of functionality lost, which may indeed lead to game-breaking-esque issues, 'cause I can't level up my characters, at least not in this way. And missions often only show up after you've completed other missions, so whatever this particular mission (I don't remember the exact name, but it's something about promotions) is hiding will stay hidden for a good while longer, it seems.

Overall, I still enjoy playing Battle Nations. Probably will for a while to come, too. I like that it's more or less part of the TF2 universe and the fact that the vast majority of the characters look like specialized Pyros. It's neat to imagine that I'm building what BLU's HQ looks like or something. It's very much a casual game, not meant to be played for long periods of time, as far as I can tell. For what it is, it does its job quite acceptably. When it doesn't its job, it's bearable but only just. It's very close to being a FaceBook game but maybe a very well-executed FaceBook game yet a FaceBook game to the end. I can't whole-heartedly recommend it because of its issues, but I'd imagine it'd be worse just saying don't even check it out. I say get it. It's not a bad game at all and can be pretty enjoyable. It's free, anyhoo. Why not?

I have been playing the iOS version of this game during my downtime over the last year. I found this to be a very fun and quite enjoyable game. The main storyline for the game is for the most part light hearted and humorous. There are however some serious points in the game. It is similar to the Facebook style games in which it takes time to build units, heal them, build buildings, and create in game materials. So playing through the missions can not be done in a single sitting, so expect to do a few missions then have to wait a day (possibly more if you have to get many different materials that will take a long time) to continue onwards. But, you can still fight random battles while you wait or play with friends.

You can also fight battles with randomly selected players (please note the other player is selected according to the strength of the soldiers you choose for the battle. So you typically won't be put up against players that are significantly stronger than you.

They have been regularly having major events (at least) since last summer. So there is plenty to do besides main storyline missions, and they also provide you a way to win nanopods.

There is "premium" in game money that is called nanopods. Nanopods are used to purchase limited time event units, special units, special buildings, to hurry units, and to heal units during battle. The easiest way to get nanopods is to symply buy them. As you level up you will earn a nanopod for each level (until you reach the level cap). You may also be given nanopods during certain missions or events. The iOS version lets you watch videos or earn the by completing tapjoy deals. Nanopods can be quite hard to come across.

I have personally never purchased nanopods. All of the nanopods I have used I got through tapjoy, watching videos, or in missions. And even then, the only time I ever needed to use a nanopod unit to win a battle was when I was level 65 and I had been playing the game for many months. You can level up your units to avoid purchasing nanopod units, but nanopod units do help in later levels. But, again, I have never purchased nanopods and I still have several of the special nanopod units.

First of all, I don't recommend this game to you if you don't have a tablet or phone. The game was mainly designed for mobile use. But other than that, the game is just amazing. Countless hours of fun and exciting storyline, a strategic and challenging combat system, enormus amount of units to find your favorite playstyle, Guild Events that require teamwork do be successful. Battle Nation was designed for mobile Phones and Tablets, what you can clearly see when playing the game. But i also need to go over a few bad things. While there is no requirement to ever pay money, there are advantages for paying player. You can buy yourself nanopods to speed up thing, but anyone that does this is an idiot. The only real use for nanos are the fact that you can buy yourself some special units that are a little bit better that their normal counterpart. Every month there is a so called Boss Strike event in the game that usually introduces a premium limited time unit that can only be purchased with nanopods for a certain time ( about 5 days). These units are very powerful and are always designed to help players with the Boss Strike if there are lacking the units to compete in it. For every enemy that you kill in this wave styled event, you get Boss Strike points, which when enough collected will give you exclusive plane units that are in the current state not being able to purchase. It's back! A relic from ages past, Battle Nations has amazingly been resurrected.

It's kinda funny how this freemium Farmville-esque game from decade ago is almost a breath of fresh air in the modern gaming epoch, but here we are!

I could've sworn bringing this game back from the dead was impossible, but Madrona Games somehow managed it. Granted, the game isn't 100% functional right now; there's a few bugs, some old and some new, but also some features like socials, such as friends and guilds, haulers, and late-game content isn't available yet. 

But again, the game just got dug out of the literal grave after over a decade, give it some time. I've got complete confidence that Madrona will do wonders with this game, nobody spends this much time and effort bringing a game back if they aren't genuinely dedicated. They even managed to get the old Steam page and Steam appid, which is why the reviews are "mixed"- that's actually from BEFORE the game shut down originally, in 2015. Check the graph, it's crazy.

As for the game, well, it's a relic from the 2010s. The gameplay revolves around turn-based combat, and resource management building out your Outpost, which is similar to Farmville. Buildings produce goods, resources, and units in real-time, which leads to a good deal of waiting around. That, and you have a premium currency, Nanopods, which are used for more advanced units and structures which help out massively. You earn a small amount for free, however. The game has a good sense of progression, and to help with that, the game has great writing and story telling.

You've been sent by the Empire to go look for uranium in the desert, and as the Captain of the 95th Rifle's Division, you're under-equipped and under-trained in a hostile wasteland. To help you out are your advisors; Lt. Morgan is your drunk, embezzling second-in-command schemer. Sgt. Ramsey is hard-headed, good-natured, and well-respected. Perkins is... Perkins. In other words, the rookie soldier that is the subject of every experiment in the Outpost. As for civilians, your liaison to them is civil engineer Floyd, who is a bleeding heart ecologist with no sense of respect for human decency. Finally, you have Zoey, your mechanic. She's talented enough to get nearly any machine working, if you count "explodes" or "catches fire everywhere" as "working." 

These characters will be your guide and the driving force in the story, for as you build up your Outpost more threats will get wind of your presence and try to drive you out. All the characters are well written to the point where modern writing in most games pales in comparison, which is again kind of weird coming from a copy of a Facebook game.

Make no mistake, Madrona's got a lot of work to do before the game is restored to it's original state, let alone a *modern* state. You can't watch ads for Nanopods anymore (thank GOD) but that leaves no way for free players to get Nanos reliably. Madrona have said they are looking into ways to help balance the economy and eventually expand the game past where it was on shutdown, and I have good faith that they'll be able to do that.

If you feel like trying the game, give it a shot; there's good reasons why fans were so dedicated they resurrected the game 10 years after it died. Here's to a long, prosperous future for Battle Nations.

Game has a promising future. Dev's remaking old, lost code. Remaking the entire game to how it was. And apparently, making moves away from the old predatory systems of the game and making it much more F2P friendly, such as converting a premium currency unit that's useless compared to others of its category (The Medium tank) and converting it to a non-premium unit. If they continue like this, It be not just a revival but a Zenkai boost.

I don't understand why there are so many negative comments to the game.  I've been playing Battle Nations on the IOS for nearly 2 years now and the game is still great!  Sure, at times the game may feel like it's Pay To Win, but the game is still playable without Nanopods. Playing without Nanopods just adds to the difficulty, which in turn adds to the fun.  The game is really fun in my opinion and I'm so happy to see the game finally in Steam!

The only complaint I have so far with the Steam version is that windowed mode isn't an option.  Hopefully in the future there will be a patch to do that.  Other than that though, the game is exactly like the IOS version, and is definitely a game you should get.

Edit: So it seems you can make it windowed by pressing the escape key and clicking on the button "Full Screen on Startup"  Figured I'd add that as I've seen a lot of people wondering how to get it to full screen.

Edit 2: So many people have been saying that this game is so much like a Facebook game so why should it be on Steam.  What exactly is so wrong with a "Facebook Game" being on Steam anyway?  I admit, you're not gonna sit down for 6 hours at a time and play Battle Nations, but the game is actually fun.  These people with not even an hour on the game and haven't played it on the IOS or any other device at all haven't really expirenced what Battle Nations really is.  The game is slow until approx. level 20, where the battles get interesting and the selection of your units make a huge difference in a fight.  With that, I again hope that everyone reading this will give Battle Nations a shot, even with all the harsh criticism coming from the opposition.

Edit 3: Nearly 6 months since this review has been made, I have gone from the top review along with all kinds of people upvotes for this game.  Now though, it's cluttered with "This game is a PTW game!  Delete now!"  I wanted to just clarify, you can go through the ENTIRE game without buying a SINGLE Nanopod.  In the IOS Version (That I played for 2 years now) has a way to get free ones by just watching 30 second videos and by downloading apps.  By now everyone has some sort of device that can run Battle Nations that they can get the free ones.  In my personal expirence, I have not spent a dime on Nanopods and have been able to progress throughout the game.

I've also seen many people say that it's a "Grind Fest" to get levels.  ....  I don't even know how to react to this.  Any game you own that has levels requires you to play and grind for levels.  Borderlands, League of Legends, Path of Exile, and many successful games all have you grinding either levels/ING Currency to get better weapons or gear.

Finally, I've stated this multiple times but just because it is an IOS game DOES NOT MAKE IT BAD.  If Clash of Clans was on Steam the amount of positive feedback would be overwhelming.  Honestly, Battle Nations is a better version of Clash of Clans.  Of course that's just my opinion and I have no facts to back that up.

I can't force any of you to try nor play this game, but I hope that I have at least covered some of the main points so that you can see the veteran fans' point of view.  Good luck and I hope to see you all on the battle field!

Here's what you need to know if you haven't heard of this game before:

1. This is a F2P game ported from mobile to Steam.
2. The game was mostly Greenlit by its existing players, myself included. I may be biased because I voted to greenlight the game and was part of the closed beta for the PC version.
3. This game is still in beta. There are crashes, the game runs in a strange windowed resolution, and some PC-specific bugs exist.

The game blends a city-building mechanic common to many F2P games with a turn based strategy game. As you collect resources in the city-building portion, you can train more troops and vehicles to use in battle. The PvP has been pretty dead for a while, and PvE events have provided the bulk of gameplay variety for a while now. The game has been incrementally updated over time, slowly increasing the level cap from 30 to 65 and adding many more buildings, UI features, resource types, enemies, locales, and most importantly, units. Level progression gets really slow around the early 20's because significant expansion is required, but once past the early 20's the game really picks up speed and units become much more interesting as you get away from 1.0 content and into more recent content.

Overall, the game starts rather slowly, but it is not difficult to succeed without buying Nanopods and the game won't punish the player for choosing not to do so. Nanopods certainly help, but the choice of whether to buy them is just that - a choice, unlike many other F2P games, especially from iOS.

Pros:

- Very likable and humorous characters and storyline. A very good mix between seriousness and comedy.
- A small, but still nice Soundtrack. Some effort went into creating those tracks.
- An easy to understand combat system that still is a lot of fun despite its simplicity.
- Regular events such as Boss Strikes, which offer great rewards for everyone participating.
- Company behind the game appears to be very involved with its community.

Cons:

- Very unstable game that keeps crashing. Very annoying.
- An interface that obviously wasn't created with PCs in mind. You will see immediately that this game was intended to be a mobile game first, before getting ported to a PC version.
- The PvP system, albeit present, isn't really worth mentioning. I hardly ever saw anyone use it. Technically, the occupation feature could be considered PvP as well, but no one ever does it to fight each other, but rather to help the occupying player to get some resources. I don't find this to be really THAT bad, but for people who look for a game in which they can bash and farm weaker players all day, this would certainly be a downer.
- You literally have to grow a big friends list and help them regularily if you don't want to wait forever to have enough resources to build something. While this, in it's principe, is good, it quickly becomes tiresome to do this every day.
- Finding a guild takes some effort, because the bad interface doesn't allow for an easy search of the existing ones. Since a lot of small and/or inactive guilds exist, finding an actual working one is quite bothersome. Took me several forum posts and tryouts to find one that wasn't utter crap.
- I find the unit info screen to be lacking. I often tried to find information there, but had to realize that it just wasn't there. And if it was, I haven't found it to this very day. Even such crucial things such as "can attack air" or "can't attack air" aren't showed there, not to mention that the unit info screen crashes 7 out of 10 times upon opening it.

tl;dr:

good game, but needs improvement in terms of bugs and interface. The world, characters, story and gameplay are good and  probably the only reason I am still sticking around, despite the bugs. It definitely has more charm than most games in this genre, now all it needs is to stop crashing all the time.

As a longtime fan of Battle Nations, I’m glad to see it return, but the current state of the game leaves a lot to be desired. Right now, several core features that made the original so engaging are missing, most notably PvP. Without PvP or other social modes like guilds and boss strikes, the game feels incomplete and loses much of its community-driven appeal.

Another concern is the absence of free-to-play nanopods, which were promised but have not been implemented. For a game built on strategic depth and community engagement, locking progression too heavily behind monetization creates frustration rather than loyalty.

Battle Nations was revived because it had a passionate, dedicated fanbase. That goodwill is being put at risk by the perception that the game is being reduced to a microtransaction platform rather than rebuilt into the rich experience players remember.

Please reconsider the direction. Restoring promised features and respecting the expectations of the community would go a long way in ensuring this revival succeeds rather than becoming another case of abandonware.

Well... it's basically the PC equivalent of a Facebook or Android game. The problem is you need special items to increase the speed of building, healing or doing whatever with your troops and buildings. You can decide to forgo that, but you'll have to wait in real-time. So if something takes five minutes, it's five minutes off your real day. 

Five minutes wouldn't be so bad if that was the extent of it, but the more advanced options can take hours or days. So unless you pay, the game's essentially stalled. 

It's not a terrible game and I've certainly played worse. Even so, that's hardly a ringing endorsement. 

That said, it's free, so if you don't believe me or think I'm full of crap, try it yourself. Maybe you'll love it, and if you do, that's great. However, I have a feeling most PC gamers won't spend a whole lot of time with this game.

I remember playing this game as a kid, but stopped after a while despite loving the characters and world.
I now remember why I stopped.

The leveling and resource scaling is just so unbalanced, it becomes borderline unplayable around level 25-30. An example is steel factories.
Steel factories require 7200 iron to be built. A warehouse allows 1000 storage. costing 75000 gold and requiring 8 people to man.  That means you need a minimum of 8 warehouses, which is 64 workers. At level 29 you get a maximum of 75 workers. Between all your different mines, food production, and army producers, you reach this number with just 5 warehouses easily. This is ignoring the extremely high cost of 600000 gold and, no joke, hundreds of hours in real time collecting the resources just to BUILD the WAREHOUSES to BUILD the FACTORY.
I haven't even mentioned the fact that the game expects you to have steel LONG before this point, giving you missions and units that require it without any possible way to obtain it - without using premium currency of course!
Technically you can collect steel from an NPC town, but that's merely 10 a day, iirc.

I really do love the funny characters, but I simply can't recommend a game that requires hundreds of hours of grinding and waiting just to get basic resources to actually play it's missions. And, honestly, I feel most who didn't grow up with it will find the combat extremely dated. Bad, even.

I really do hope extreme balance efforts are made, because I would be willing to grind (within reason) to see more of these characters and stories.

Battle Nations has a lot going for it, great art, simple combat and the Steam version has Team Fortress 2 characters. On the surface this is a Farmvillian 'click harvest' sort of game that wants you to buy micro currency called nano pods. These nano pods let you finish tasks instantly instead of waiting X amount of seconds, minutes or hours. You can also buy the good units with nano pods. If you don't want to buy nano pods, you can slowly get them, maybe one per level you achieve.

With that out of the way, this game sets itself apart from other click to harvest games by having simple tactical strategy combat. Its your army vs enemies. Before each battle, you pick X amount of soldiers and place them on the battle grid. For the most part, on your side, each grid seems to be 3 rows of 5 with the last row only having 3. Each type of unit / soldier has a different attack range and pattern. Some troops can only attack the first row of enemies. Others can attack up to two rows. Some units can attack the entire row or every enemy on the grid as long as its not being obscured. There are fire units that cause burn damage as the battle goes on. If all of your units are out of ammo or 'cooling down,' you can 'pass' a turn.

Once the battle starts, the units cannot be moved. When a row of units has been cleared, the rows move up. So when the front line dies, the next line becomes the new front line. Combat is turn based. You go once, then the enemy goes, then you go. Like a game of chess where you only do one attack instead of a RPG that might have your entire party take a turn before the enemy gets its turn. Each attack has a cool down that lasts one or two turns. Its a very simple system. Easy for kids, easy to play. The enemy AI seems random. They won't make intelligent attack patterns like this unit is hurt, let's finish him off!

When a unit is 'injured' (finished off), you will need to visit your hospital and admit them into the hospital. Its not just automatic. It just feels like an extra clicking process, when really the game could just have a courtesy to put them into the hospital for you even if it takes X number of minutes to fully heal them. Units that are not 'injured' get full health for the next battle, which is great. It seems like a courtesy when everything is click heavy.

When units get enough experience from battles, they can be promoted (leveled up), which takes X amount of hours. Once upgraded, they have improved stats, other bonuses and even additional attacks. It adds some nice depth to a simple game and rewards players who put in the time or nano pods.

If you'd like a real combat challenge, eventually the game will let you post a battle flag so you can have Player vs Player. In PvP each player gets 20 seconds to take a turn, which keeps the battle active. When you've used a unit in a Player vs Player battle, you can no longer use that unit for X number of hours until they 'return,' but if you use nano pods... This makes a need to buy more units from your barracks and pay nano pods for the better units. If you accomplish a mission while in a player vs player battle it kicks you out of the battle, denying you a victory bonus. The plus side is that if a unit dies in battle against another player, you don't need to restore them from the hospital. They just come back with the others fully healed.

It is player vs player that I enjoy, that keeps me coming back every 2+ hours to play it. Facing real people and having to chose, do I make an A+ team to take on an unknown team and have only C units for my next team? Or do I make two B+ teams for two battles? Usually I can win the first two battles, before my good units are used up. The good units are the ones that cost nanopods, but the game gives you one or so of each good unit, so you know just how good they are compared to the rest. When those good units die outside of player vs player, they cost a lot of gold + metal to heal them in the hospital. With that in mind, I rarely use my good units in non PvP.

Now that I've covered the actual game part, let me cover the 'click harvest' half of the game. It feels like every other click harvest game. You have an 'Outpost' and several types of buildings. You have expand your land, setup military buildings, shops, homes, resource gathering and place decorations. Homes (camps, houses) will increase your worker capacity and get you gold from 'taxes.' Decorations will boost resources you gather from nearby buildings. Such as flowers will get you 8% more gold from surrounding homes. Military buildings like Barracks, factories and so on will build units. Resources will let you gather things like stone, lumber and oil. Having gardens, raising crops, tool shops, building tools and bakeries baking goods will all get you gold. The problem is you need to click to harvest the output of ea in X amount of hours.

All buildings can be upgraded, but you can only upgrade one building at a time, unless you use nano pods. Upgrading buildings makes them more efficient and gives higher output. Clicking things seems a lot like busy work and that's part of the fun of building your own outpost, because you took the time to get it.  Sure you can sink a lot of time into this game, Farmville or the Simpsons, but there's a certain point where it becomes too demanding like a bad habit.

I've been playing 5+ hours and I still haven't gotten to any Team Fortress 2 characters. They reserve those characters for level 10 players. Want to know how I know? It will tell you with full screen billboards. Not just billboards for those characters, but full page ads saying for $5 you get X amount of nano pods and we'll throw in 10,000 gold! These billboards appear frequently and I need to click 'no thanks.' I started taking screenshots of them and I wonder if Steam will bust me for screenshots of spam, when its in game.

The game also seems a little crash heavy, I've got 3 computers that I play this on and while some crashes seem to be random, it crashes pretty consistently when I try to view detailed information on a unit. If others are having this problem, it can prevent them from getting beyond level 6.

The character art is a high point of this game and goes a long way to make me enjoy it anymore. With every new objective, you'll read short lines of dialog from them and after you complete an objective, you'll read more brief dialog and see what you earned. To be honest, I didn't read the dialog when there's an easy to follow objective list bluntly telling you, build this, upgrade that, visit here and battle that. The dialog seems needless and just more clicking even if they could be reciting the best lines you've ever heard. The mission list is easy to follow, but after you click a mission, to open the objectives, then you need to close the list and do it, when the game could easily just have a button to instantly do it so you don't need to exit and find it. Of course if there was some easy click button it would cost nano pods.

In the future I'd appreciate easier clicking so I don't have to scroll around to find everything and click on it. Any developer could easily make a long list of 'countdowns' so that I can easily see what's doing what and a harvest everything button that has been cooled down, but again that would probably cost nano pods to do something so courteously easy for the player. I guess being convenient for a player doesn't generate revenue.

In all, there is an actual game here its not just click to harvest, but there are other click harvest games and other tactical strategy games that seem deeper with better AI. It will keep you coming back day after day to harvest things and play, but make you feel like you're missing out when you don't have the better units that cost nano pods. The game gives you good units, but if you want more of those good units, you'll need nano pods. Without the potential for Team Fortress 2 characters, I would have lost interest.
